title: Unmeasurable metrics: what you can't measure even in retrospect, so don't set goals on it
summary: Jason Cohen argues that some enticing metrics can't be measured even after the fact, so you shouldn't predict them or turn them into goals. Examples: single-feature revenue impact, incremental churn initiatives, risk probabilities, brand value, culture ROI. Use KPIs that measure specific aspects of your systems instead.

principles.text: If a metric can't be measured in retrospect, it can't be measured now, predicted, or used as a goal.
principles.quote: If they cannot be measured in retrospect, they cannot be measured now, and you certainly cannot predict them or make a goal from them.

principles.text: You can't attribute revenue to individual features; usage is a valid KPI but not the same as revenue.
principles.quote: Even after the fact, with 100s of 1000s of customers (in our case at WP Engine), it's still not possible to attribute revenue to individual features.

principles.text: Rare events like small churn changes drown in noise: a 10% churn cut from 3% to 2.7% is below normal monthly variance.
principles.quote: If churn is 3%/mo, an initiative that reduces churn by 10%--a big impact!--will result in 2.7%/mo. How hard is it to measure a difference of 0.3%, month over month?

principles.text: Churn lags action: customers leaving today decided weeks or months ago, so new initiatives can't change them.
principles.quote: An activity you start today is unlikely to change the trajectory of customers who have already decided to leave, and only today happened to push the red button.

principles.text: Still work on churn even though single initiatives can't be measured, because retention compounds and SaaS profit comes in later years.
principles.quote: retention compounds, and all the profit generated by a customer of a SaaS business happens in the later years

principles.text: Don't put probabilities on a risk slide; one-off independent risks can never be validated. List only risks worth action or awareness.
principles.quote: So don't put probabilities on the slide at all. Only list the risks that you feel are so important that they either merit action or awareness.
